answer:
No—the published BLEU gap alone cannot isolate the architectural effect, because the papers report different beam widths and length adjustments rather than a decoding-controlled comparison. [S:173159a1bb15#53] [S:14467d21708c#44]

- **1706.03762v7.pdf, p.8:** reports beam width **4** and length penalty **α = 0.6**, with no different decoding settings stated for base versus big models: “We used beam search with a beam size of 4 and length penalty α = 0.6 [38].” The settings were selected on the development set; maximum output length was input length + 50, with early termination when possible. [S:173159a1bb15#53]
- **1705.03122v3.pdf, p.5:** reports beam width **5**: “We use a beam of width 5.” For WMT’14 English–German, it tunes the length-normalization constant on newstest2015 and divides log-likelihoods by |y|^α: “For WMT’14 English-German we tune a length normalization constant on a separate development set (newstest2015) and we nor- malize log-likelihoods by |y|α (Wu et al., 2016).” The supplied passage does not give the selected numerical α. [S:14467d21708c#44]

Both papers therefore adjust scores for length, but the evidence does not establish identical adjustment formulas or strengths, and their beam widths differ; attributing the BLEU gap solely to architecture would leave these decoding differences uncontrolled. [S:173159a1bb15#53] [S:14467d21708c#44] Moreover, “attention instead of convolution” is an incomplete description of the comparison: 1705.03122v3.pdf, p.2 explicitly says, “We also use attention in every decoder layer”. [S:14467d21708c#9]

The original SQuAD contained **107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles**, while SQuAD 2.0 added **53,775 new unanswerable questions** about the same paragraphs (1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 2: “SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles”; 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 2: “with 53,775 new, unanswerable questions about the same paragraphs.”). [S:8484660c7932#6] [S:0bff9579041a#9]

In 1606.05250v3.pdf, the original questions were crowdsourced from Wikipedia articles, with answers drawn as text spans from the corresponding passages (p. 2: “questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to ev- ery question is a segment of text, or span, from the corresponding reading passage.”). [S:8484660c7932#6] For development and test evaluation, the original paper also collected at least two additional answers per question, asking crowdworkers to select the shortest answering span (p. 4: “we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question”; “asked to select the shortest span in the para- graph that answered the question.”). [S:8484660c7932#22]

In 1806.03822v1.pdf, the new unanswerable questions were crafted with two challenging properties: **relevance to the paragraph** and **a plausible answer span of the requested type** (p. 2: “Crowdworkers crafted these questions so that (1) they are relevant to the para- graph, and (2) the paragraph contains a plausible answer—something of the same type as what the question asks for.”). [S:0bff9579041a#9] Relevance prevents simple word-overlap heuristics from distinguishing answerable and unanswerable questions (p. 2: “Otherwise, simple heuristics (e.g., based on word overlap) could distinguish answerable and unanswerable questions”). [S:0bff9579041a#11] Plausible answers supply distracting candidate spans (p. 7: “the plausible answers in our dataset do indeed serve their purpose of be- ing distracting spans that could be mistaken for the correct answer.”). [S:0bff9579041a#54]

The follow-up therefore extends the original task to require abstention when the paragraph supports no answer (1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 1: “systems must not only answer questions when possible, but also determine when no answer is supported by the paragraph and abstain from answering.”). [S:0bff9579041a#1] The reported counts measure different things: the original count covers question-answer pairs, whereas the added count covers new unanswerable questions (1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 2: “107,785 question-answer pairs”; 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 2: “53,775 new, unanswerable questions”). [S:8484660c7932#6] [S:0bff9579041a#9]

entire article. Over the development and test sets,
2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at
least one of the additional crowdworkers.

Extractive reading comprehension sys-
tems can often locate the correct answer to
a question in a context document, but they
also tend to make unreliable guesses on
questions for which the correct answer is
not stated in the context. Existing datasets
either focus exclusively on answerable
questions, or use automatically generated
unanswerable questions that are easy to
identify. To address these weaknesses, we
present SQuAD 2.0, the latest version of
the Stanford Question Answering Dataset
(SQuAD). SQuAD 2.0 combines exist-
ing SQuAD data with over 50,000 unan-
swerable questions written adversarially
by crowdworkers to look similar to an-
swerable ones. To do well on SQuAD 2.0,
systems must not only answer questions
when possible, but also determine when no
answer is supported by the paragraph and
abstain from answering. SQuAD 2.0 is a

The supplied evidence establishes **83.1% ImageNet top-1 for non-distilled DeiT-B at 384 resolution**, but omits the original ViT paper’s JFT-pretrained ViT-L/16 accuracy, so the numerical gap cannot be verified (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.14: “DeiT-B↑384 83.1”). [S:d3fbb331ee87#54]

- **ViT data and resolution:** The original ViT paper identifies the model as pretrained on JFT-300M (2010.11929v2.pdf, p.5: “The smaller ViT-L/16 model pre-trained on JFT-300M”). [S:4efdd1839269#37] Its ImageNet results use fine-tuning at resolution 512 (2010.11929v2.pdf, p.5: “For ImageNet results in Table 2, we ﬁne-tuned at higher resolution: 512 for ViT-L/16”). [S:4efdd1839269#34] ImageNet is listed as a fine-tuning dataset (2010.11929v2.pdf, p.14: “Dataset Steps Base LR ImageNet 20 000”). [S:4efdd1839269#98]
- **DeiT data and resolution:** The DeiT paper uses ImageNet alone (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.2: “It uses Imagenet as the sole training set”). [S:d3fbb331ee87#6] Its notation identifies ↑384 as larger-resolution fine-tuning and separately marks distilled models with an alembic, supporting identification of the 83.1% row as non-distilled (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.8: “When we ﬁne-tune DeiT at a larger resolution, we append the resulting operating resolution at the end, e.g, DeiT-B↑384. Last, when using our distillation procedure, we identify it with an alembic sign as DeiT⚗”). [S:d3fbb331ee87#34]

**These results do not isolate a single design choice:** model size, operating resolution, data regime and training procedure vary simultaneously, as the following evidence establishes. ViT-L/16 is the Large variant (2010.11929v2.pdf, p.5: “ViT-L/16 means the ‘Large’ variant with 16×16 input patch size”). [S:4efdd1839269#32] DeiT-B instead shares ViT-B’s architecture (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.8: “DeiT-B, which has the same architecture as ViT-B”). [S:d3fbb331ee87#34] The DeiT comparison table lists 307M parameters for ViT-L/16 and 86M for DeiT-B↑384 (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.12: “ViT-L/16 [15] 307M”; “DeiT-B↑384 86M”). [S:d3fbb331ee87#49] The original ViT procedure uses Adam pretraining, momentum-SGD fine-tuning and parameter averaging (2010.11929v2.pdf, p.5: “We train all models, including ResNets, using Adam”; “For ﬁne-tuning we use SGD with momentum”; “also used Polyak & Juditsky (1992) averaging with a factor of 0.9999”). [S:4efdd1839269#34] DeiT additionally emphasizes extensive augmentation (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.15: “we rely on extensive data augmentation”; “after ablation we choose Rand-Augment instead of AutoAugment”). [S:d3fbb331ee87#61] Thus, attributing any accuracy difference solely to architecture or distillation would require a controlled comparison absent from the supplied evidence.
